title: US Firm Accused of Firing Entire 80-Member Indian Support Team on 5-Minute Call
excerpt: According to an employee's viral account, a US-based company — described in reports as a bank — dismissed its whole Indian customer service team in a single brief Google Meet call. The allegation has not been independently verified.
body:
• An employee alleged in a viral social media post that a US-based company laid off its entire Indian customer service team — 80 people — during a five-minute Google Meet call.
  • Moneycontrol describes the company as a US bank; the firm was not publicly named in the reports, and the claim has not been independently verified.
  • The allegation was reported by the Hindustan Times, NDTV, Moneycontrol, Gulf News and Inshorts over September 16–17.
  • The episode echoes a pattern of video-call mass layoffs, from Better.com's 2021 Zoom firings to a 2024 two-minute Google Meet call that ended a 200-person startup.

The Allegation

According to an employee's account that went viral on social media, a US-based company summoned its entire Indian customer service team to a Google Meet call and dismissed all 80 of them within about five minutes. The worker described the layoff as abrupt and impersonal, and the post drew a wave of reactions online ranging from sympathy to skepticism.

Moneycontrol describes the employer as a US bank. The company was not publicly named in the reporting, and none of the details — the headcount, the length of the call, or the circumstances — have been independently verified. What is established is that multiple news outlets treated the employee's account as newsworthy enough to report, with careful attribution to the worker's version of events.

A Familiar Playbook

If the account is accurate, the method would hardly be unprecedented. In January 2024, the online rental platform Frontdesk laid off its entire 200-person workforce during a "two-minute Google Meet call." In late 2021, Better.com CEO Vishal Garg fired 900 employees over Zoom, an episode that drew global condemnation. And in October 2025, an Indian employee of a different US firm described a three-minute call in which the company's COO, cameras and microphones disabled, announced that most of the Indian workforce was being let go as part of an "internal organisational restructuring" — with no questions allowed.

The through line is the format: a calendar invite with no warning, a brief scripted announcement, and a call that ends before anyone can respond. Labor advocates have long argued that the practice strips layoffs of even the minimal dignity of a conversation.

Why Support Teams Are Exposed

Customer service roles sit at the intersection of two forces squeezing offshore teams: cost restructuring and automation. As artificial intelligence takes over routine support queries, banks and tech firms have been shrinking the human teams that once handled them. Amazon confirmed plans to cut nearly 14,000 corporate jobs amid its AI push, and industry analyses have flagged customer support among the roles most exposed to automation.

For offshore support operations — long a cost advantage for US firms — the combination means headcount is under pressure from both the finance department and the technology roadmap.

Diaspora Angle

Tens of thousands of Indian professionals staff customer service and back-office operations for US companies, often working remotely across time zones. When an entire team can allegedly be dissolved in a five-minute call, it underscores how precarious that arrangement can be: workers far from headquarters, with little visibility into decisions made about their jobs and limited recourse when the decision arrives by video link.

What's Next

The immediate questions are basic and unanswered: which company is involved, whether it will confirm or contest the employee's account, and what severance — if any — the affected workers received. Until then, the story stands as an allegation, not an established fact. But the attention it has drawn suggests a broader anxiety it has tapped: in an era of AI-driven efficiency drives, the video-call layoff has become a symbol of how disposable even large, functioning teams can feel.
